History of computers, part 1 - The bulletin board system

When I got my first PC in 1991 (I only had a TI994/A before that), an IBM PS/1 286, I was blissfully ignorant of how computers worked until my friend showed me how to connect to his own friend's BBS. I didn't know a thing about ANSI and connected to BBSs using a terminal program in Microsoft Works 2.0 which neglected to display all of the art properly. Eventually, I discovered YaleBBS and colour and thought it was the bee's knees until someone pointed out that all BBS' looked the way that YaleBBS did but that you had to use a decent communications program like Telix. Anyway, most of what I ended up learning about how computers worked came from communicating with other people on BBSs and frankly, that knowledge has opened up a plethora of doors for me.

I am interested in re-learning to sew, what kind of machine would you suggest?
I'm no expert, but you'd probably be fine trying any functioning machine at some used goods store. Would certainly be affordable, low-risk if it breaks or is insufficient, due to the lower price.

Old fashioned steel bodied machine.

80s Kenmore's are easy to use and were abundant enough that they can easily be bought for cheap and repaired. Expect to spend about $75-$100 for machine and repairs. As long as you take care of it, it will never die.

Few new machines are worth buying unless you get a Viking or a baby lock.

My baby lock is old (Model B21) and still a nimble work horse so I definitely recommend them. Mine's very simple (nothing digital/computerized) so @Roe_beans I think you'd be ok with buying a used one.

I got my computerized Kenmore about 12 years ago, and it runs like a champ. It has enclosed ball bearing mechanical parts, so it doesn't need to be oiled. I've never had to get it serviced--it runs so smoothly. The only time I had trouble with it was when I nicked the footplate by sewing heavy duty stuff (I pushed the needle all over the place, trying to get the work sewn), and a piece of metal shaving was interfering with the needle and threading. My husband figured that out, filed the shaving down, I replaced the needle, and it was all good! When I received this machine as a beginner sewer, I was a little intimidated by all of the stitches. As I've grown in my sewing skills, I've come to appreciate the more complicated stitches and all of the options that the machine has to offer.

I've seen really nice computerized Brother machines at Costco for good deals. I think Jo Ann Fabrics also does a machine sale around black Friday/Christmas time too. Happy shopping!
